claim: The first dental generation in catshark develops relatively superficially on the oral surface before the dental lamina has fully invaginated.
source: The first dental generation develops relatively superficially on the oral surface before the dental lamina has fully invaginated (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by histological images in Figure 1D showing early tooth development at the oral surface.

claim: New teeth are initiated at the tip of the dental lamina and move anteriorly in a conveyor belt-like manner in catshark.
source: New teeth are initiated at the tip of the dental lamina and move anteriorly in a conveyor belt-like manner.
evidence: Stated as an observation from the study of catshark tooth development.

claim: Adjacent tooth families in catshark are staggered in the timing of their initiation.
source: Adjacent tooth families are staggered in the timing of their initiation (Figure 1C, J and L), resulting in differences in the developmental stages of adjacent teeth.
evidence: Supported by images showing staggered tooth development patterns.

claim: Embryonic catshark teeth generally develop with 3 cusps.
source: Embryonic teeth generally develop with 3 cusps (Figure 1C, J and K).
evidence: Supported by images of embryonic catshark teeth showing tricuspid morphology.

claim: Adult catsharks can possess anywhere between 3 and 7 cusps depending on the position of the tooth along the jaw margin.
source: In contrast, adult catsharks can possess anywhere between 3 and 7 cusps depending on the position of the tooth along the jaw margin (Figure 1F–I).
evidence: Supported by images of adult catshark teeth showing variable cusp numbers.

claim: fgf10 is expressed in a highly restricted manner to only a few epithelial cells at the tip of the developing catshark tooth during cap stage.
source: The expression of fgf10 is highly restricted to only a few epithelial cells at the tip of the developing tooth, during cap stage (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data showing restricted fgf10 expression.

claim: fgf10 expression in catshark is located precisely within a small cluster of non-proliferative dental epithelial cells marked by a lack of PCNA expression.
source: This expression is located precisely within a small cluster of non-proliferative dental epithelial cells (Figure 4Ab), marked by a lack of PCNA expression (Figure 4Aa).
evidence: Supported by double in situ/immunohistochemistry showing co-localization of fgf10 with non-proliferative cells.

claim: The expression of fgf10 in catshark is almost identical to that in the opossum (Monodelphis domestica).
source: Interestingly, the expression of fgf3 and fgf10 is almost identical between the shark and the opossum (Monodelphis domestica), which shows a subtle shift in expression of Fgf10 compared to placental mammals, with Fgf10 expressed in both the EK and the underlying dental mesenchyme in the opossum, and not in the EK of the mouse (Kettunen et al., 2000; Moustakas et al., 2011).
evidence: Comparison with published data on opossum Fgf10 expression patterns.

claim: Loss of Fgf10 in the EK in placental mammals is a lineage-specific modification in EK signalling.
source: The similarity in expression between marsupial mammals and sharks raises the possibility that loss of Fgf10 in the EK in placental mammals is a lineage-specific modification in EK signalling.
evidence: Inferred from comparative expression patterns across species.

claim: bmp4 is absent from the apical tip of the dental epithelium throughout dental morphogenesis in catshark.
source: Unlike dkk1 and fgf10, bmp4 is absent from the apical tip of the dental epithelium throughout dental morphogenesis (Db and Eb).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data showing bmp4 expression patterns.

claim: bmp4 expression is rapidly downregulated within the apical tip of the catshark tooth.
source: However, we do not observe any secondary upregulation within the putative EK in the catshark. Instead, its expression is rapidly downregulated within the apical tip of the tooth (Figure 3I; Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data showing bmp4 downregulation at the apex.

claim: The region of bmp4 downregulation in catshark corresponds specifically to a restricted group of non-proliferative epithelial cells.
source: This region of bmp4 downregulation corresponds specifically to a restricted group of non-proliferative epithelial cells (Figure 4Dc).
evidence: Supported by double in situ/immunohistochemistry showing correlation with PCNA-negative cells.

claim: bmp4 becomes further restricted to only the lateral epithelial cells of the developing catshark tooth throughout later stages of morphogenesis.
source: Throughout later stages of morphogenesis, bmp4 becomes further restricted to only the lateral epithelial cells of the developing tooth (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data at later developmental stages.

claim: mdk is expressed within the apical tip of developing catshark teeth corresponding to the putative EK-like signalling centre.
source: Midkine (mdk) has previously been observed within the apical tip of developing teeth in the catshark (S. canicula) and little skate (Leucoraja erinacea), corresponding to the putative EK-like signalling centre (Rasch et al., 2020; Rasch et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from previous studies on mdk expression in chondrichthyans.

claim: mdk has an overlapping expression pattern to fgf3 in both the apical epithelial cells and the underlying mesenchymal papilla in catshark.
source: We find mdk with an overlapping expression pattern to fgf3 in both the apical epithelial cells and the underlying mesenchymal papilla (Figure 3N)
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data showing mdk expression pattern.

claim: shh is found early in tooth bud formation, exclusively within the apical tip of the dental epithelium in catshark.
source: whilst shh is found early in tooth bud formation, exclusively within the apical tip of the dental epithelium (Figure 3O; Figure 2G) before its expansion throughout the inner dental epithelium (Figure 2H, I).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data showing shh expression at early stages.

claim: isl1 expression is only observed in a few apical cells associated with the putative primary EK in catshark.
source: Another marker with a similar and restricted expression pattern to fgf10 is isl1 (Figure 3P). isl1 expression is only observed in a few apical cells associated with the putative primary EK.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data showing restricted isl1 expression.

claim: Canonical Wnt signalling plays a crucial role in the formation of dental cusps in mammals.
source: Canonical Wnt signalling plays a crucial role in the formation of dental cusps in mammals (Kratochwil et al., 2002; Liu et al., 2008).
evidence: Cited from previous studies on Wnt signalling in mammalian tooth development.

claim: lef1 is expressed within developing bell stage catshark teeth.
source: In the catshark, the transcription factor lymphoid enhancer binding factor-1 (lef1) (Figure 3A) and the transcriptional co-factor β-catenin (Figure 3B) are both expressed within developing bell stage teeth.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data showing lef1 expression.

claim: β-catenin is expressed within developing bell stage catshark teeth.
source: In the catshark, the transcription factor lymphoid enhancer binding factor-1 (lef1) (Figure 3A) and the transcriptional co-factor β-catenin (Figure 3B) are both expressed within developing bell stage teeth.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data showing β-catenin expression.

claim: There is an observable upregulation of lef1 and β-catenin expression within the apical dental epithelium in catshark.
source: However, there is also an observable upregulation of their expression within the apical dental epithelium (Figure 3: white arrowhead).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data showing upregulated expression at the apex.

claim: wnt11 is upregulated specifically within the apical dental epithelium during cap stage in catshark.
source: We note the upregulation of wnt11 specifically within the apical dental epithelium during cap stage (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data showing wnt11 expression.

claim: axin2 is expressed within the early dental epithelium in catshark but its expression is not specifically restricted to the apex.
source: The downstream target of canonical Wnt signalling, axin2, is also expressed within the early dental epithelium; however, its expression is not specifically restricted to the apex (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data showing axin2 expression pattern.

claim: dkk1 is expressed within both the dental papilla and throughout the dental epithelium in late morphogenesis in catshark.
source: dkk1 is seen within both the dental papilla and throughout the dental epithelium in late morphogenesis (Figures 3E and 4C).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data showing dkk1 expression pattern.

claim: During cap stage in catshark, dkk1 epithelial expression is specifically restricted to the non-proliferative cells corresponding to the putative EK.
source: Although dkk1 is expressed throughout the entire dental epithelium during late morphogenesis (Figure 3E), during cap stage its epithelial expression is specifically restricted to the non-proliferative cells corresponding to the putative EK (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by double in situ/immunohistochemistry showing dkk1 in PCNA-negative cells.

claim: sfrp3 is specifically restricted to the dental mesenchyme in catshark, with weak expression within the dental papilla.
source: In contrast to dkk1, sfrp3 is specifically restricted to the dental mesenchyme, with weak expression within the dental papilla (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data showing sfrp3 expression pattern.

claim: smad1 is expressed within the putative EK at the tip of the developing catshark tooth.
source: smad1 (Figure 3J) is expressed within the putative EK at the tip of the developing tooth
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data showing smad1 expression.

claim: smad3 is expressed throughout the dental epithelium and dental mesenchyme in catshark.
source: whilst smad3 (Figure 3K) and smad7 (Figure 3L) are both expressed throughout the dental epithelium and dental mesenchyme.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data showing smad3 expression pattern.

claim: smad7 is expressed throughout the dental epithelium and dental mesenchyme in catshark.
source: whilst smad3 (Figure 3K) and smad7 (Figure 3L) are both expressed throughout the dental epithelium and dental mesenchyme.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data showing smad7 expression pattern.

claim: bambi is expressed in both dental epithelium and dental papilla in catshark.
source: Furthermore, as with smad7, BMP and activin membrane-bound inhibitor (bambi) is expressed in both dental epithelium and dental papilla (Figure 3M).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data showing bambi expression pattern.

claim: bmp4 expression is visible throughout the dental papilla but appears absent from the dental epithelium in whole mount catshark samples.
source: bmp4 expression is visible throughout the dental papilla, but appears absent from the dental epithelium (A', A'', B', and B'').
evidence: Supported by whole mount in situ hybridization data.

claim: fgf3 expression is strongly upregulated within both primary EKs and secondary EKs in catshark.
source: fgf3 expression is strongly upregulated within both primary EKs (D': black arrowheads) and secondary EKs (C', C'', D', and D'': white arrowheads).
evidence: Supported by whole mount in situ hybridization data showing fgf3 expression at cusp sites.

claim: shh expression is present within both the primary EKs and secondary EKs in catshark.
source: Although its expression is not restricted to the EK throughout morphogenesis, clear shh expression present within both the primary EKs (E' and F': black arrowheads) and secondary EKs (E', E'', and F'': white arrowheads).
evidence: Supported by whole mount in situ hybridization data showing shh expression at cusp sites.

claim: fgf10 expression is restricted to the future cusp forming primary and secondary EKs in catshark.
source: As with fgf3, fgf10 expression is also restricted to the future cusp forming primary (G' and G'': black arrowheads) and secondary EKs (G' and G'': white arrowhead), however its expression does not extend into the dental mesenchyme.
evidence: Supported by whole mount in situ hybridization data showing fgf10 expression pattern.

claim: IWR-1-endo functions through stabilising cytoplasmic Axin2, leading to a decrease in canonical Wnt signalling.
source: IWR-1-endo is a canonical Wnt antagonist. It functions through stabilising cytoplasmic Axin2, in turn increasing proteasome-mediated degradation of cytoplasmic β-catenin, leading to a decrease in canonical Wnt signalling (Chen et al., 2009).
evidence: Cited from published mechanism of IWR-1-endo action.

claim: CHIR99021 selectively inhibits the kinase activity of GSK3, leading to a stabilisation of cytoplasmic β-catenin and a subsequent increase in canonical Wnt signalling.
source: In contrast, CHIR99021 selectively inhibits the kinase activity of GSK3 (Ring et al., 2003). This prevents the formation of the β-catenin destruction complex and in turn leads to a stabilisation of cytoplasmic β-catenin and a subsequent increase in canonical Wnt signalling (Wagman et al., 2004).
evidence: Cited from published mechanism of CHIR99021 action.

claim: There is a significant effect of treatment on overall tooth shape in catshark following Wnt perturbation.
source: After carrying out a general Procrustes analysis (GPA), we found a significant effect of treatment on overall tooth shape (Procrustes ANOVA: R2=0.09174, F2,115=8.2771, p<0.001), whilst controlling for variation within samples.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of geometric morphometric data.

claim: There is a significant effect of sample on tooth shape in catshark following Wnt perturbation.
source: We also found a significant effect of sample on shape (Procrustes ANOVA: R2=0.27092, F20,115=2.4442, p<0.001), highlighting variation found within sample measurements.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of geometric morphometric data.

claim: 58.3% of the variation in tooth shape observed between catshark samples can be explained by PC1.
source: PCA revealed that 58.3% of the variation in tooth shape observed between samples can be explained by a single axis of variation (PC1), with a further 13.8% explained by a second axis of variation (PC2) (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by principal component analysis of morphometric data.

claim: There is a significant effect of treatment on centroid size in catshark teeth following Wnt perturbation.
source: Following treatment, we found a significant effect of treatment on centroid size (ANOVA: F2,115=235.5886, p<0.001), whilst controlling for variation within samples (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of centroid size measurements.

claim: There is a significant decrease in centroid size (–35.9%) following IWR-1-endo treatment in catshark teeth.
source: There is a significant decrease in centroid size (–35.9%) following IWR-1-endo treatment (Tukey: p<0.001)
evidence: Supported by post hoc statistical analysis of centroid size data.

claim: There is a significant increase in centroid size (+12.8%) as a result of CHIR99021 treatment in catshark teeth relative to control samples.
source: whilst conversely there is a significant increase in centroid size (+12.8%) as a result of CHIR99021 treatment relative to control samples (Tukey: p<0.001) (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by post hoc statistical analysis of centroid size data.

claim: IWR-1-endo treatment resulted in stunted catshark teeth that failed to undergo normal morphogenesis yet successfully underwent mineralisation.
source: IWR-1-endo treatment resulted in stunted teeth, with the developed teeth failing to undergo normal morphogenesis, yet successfully undergoing mineralisation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by images of treated catshark teeth.

claim: Most lateral catshark teeth following IWR-1-endo treatment exhibit a reduction in secondary cusp size, with some teeth exhibiting a unicuspid morphology with a complete loss of secondary cusps.
source: Most lateral teeth exhibit a reduction in secondary cusp size, with some teeth exhibiting a unicuspid morphology with a complete loss of secondary cusps.
evidence: Supported by observations of treated catshark teeth.

claim: Upregulation of canonical Wnt signalling via CHIR99021 treatment resulted in catshark teeth more similar in appearance to the standard catshark dentition.
source: In contrast, upregulation of canonical Wnt signalling via CHIR99021 treatment resulted in teeth more similar in appearance to the standard catshark dentition.
evidence: Supported by observations of treated catshark teeth.

claim: Lateral CHIR99021-treated catshark teeth are clearly larger and wider than controls.
source: Lateral CHIR99021 teeth (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and Figure 6—figure supplement 4) are clearly larger and wider than controls (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Supported by images of treated catshark teeth.

claim: The proportion of catshark teeth exhibiting fourth cusps is significantly lower in control samples (1%) than CHIR99021-treated samples (12%).
source: However, the proportion of teeth exhibiting fourth cusps is significantly lower in control samples (1%), than CHIR99021-treated samples (12%) (chi-square: χ-squared=16.887, df = 1, p-value < 0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of cusp number data.

claim: Changing the width of the initial tooth site (Bwi) together with activator-autoactivation (Act) in the ToothMaker model is capable of recreating 5 and 6 cusped catshark teeth.
source: When attempting to simulate this increase in cusp number, we observed that changing the width of the initial tooth site (Bwi) together with activator-autoactivation (Act) is capable of recreating 5 and 6 cusped teeth (Figure 8E–F).
evidence: Supported by in silico modeling results.

claim: Decreasing the activator auto-activation (Act) in the ToothMaker model resulted in unicuspid phenotypes strikingly like IWR-1-endo-treated catshark samples.
source: Both decreasing the activator auto-activation (Act) (seal baseline: Act = 0.1; shark baseline: Act = 0.25) or increasing the inhibition of the activator (Inh) (seal baseline: Inh = 8; shark baseline: Inh 52) (Figure 9A and D) resulted in unicuspid phenotypes strikingly like IWR-1-endo-treated samples (Figure 9G).
evidence: Supported by in silico modeling results compared to experimental data.

claim: Increasing the inhibition of the activator (Inh) in the ToothMaker model resulted in unicuspid phenotypes strikingly like IWR-1-endo-treated catshark samples.
source: Both decreasing the activator auto-activation (Act) (seal baseline: Act = 0.1; shark baseline: Act = 0.25) or increasing the inhibition of the activator (Inh) (seal baseline: Inh = 8; shark baseline: Inh 52) (Figure 9A and D) resulted in unicuspid phenotypes strikingly like IWR-1-endo-treated samples (Figure 9G).
evidence: Supported by in silico modeling results compared to experimental data.

claim: Sharks possess a comparable EK-like signalling centre to the mammalian EK.
source: Overall, our results demonstrate that signalling centres comparable to mammalian EKs are present in the shark during tooth morphogenesis.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence including gene expression and functional studies.

claim: The fundamental components of the EK signalling centre are highly conserved between catshark and mammals.
source: Our results reveal that despite differences in molecular signalling between the catshark and mammals, the fundamental components of the EK signalling centre are highly conserved.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comparative gene expression analysis.

claim: EK signalling at the apex of the developing tooth cusp is a vertebrate innovation.
source: Therefore, EK signalling at the apex of the developing tooth cusp is a vertebrate innovation and contributes to the vast range of vertebrate dental phenotypes.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comparative analysis across vertebrate lineages.

claim: A common set of developmental principles account for tooth morphogenesis between mammals and sharks.
source: Overall our data imply that a common set of developmental principles account for tooth morphogenesis between mammals and sharks.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence including gene expression, functional studies, and modeling.

claim: The basic developmental principles of mammalian tooth morphogenesis are shared with sharks.
source: Therefore, we suggest that the basic developmental principles of mammalian tooth morphogenesis are shared with sharks, and that perhaps shark tooth shape variation can be modelled with the same developmental principles.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comparative analysis and modeling results.

claim: The expression of fgf3, fgf10, and shh in catshark marks the onset of the primary EK-like signalling.
source: Importantly, the superficial nature of expression in these three genes is associated with the initiation of the first tooth placode (Figure 2A, D and G), and this could in fact mark the onset of the primary EK-like signalling in the shark tooth
evidence: Inference drawn from gene expression patterns at early tooth development stages.

claim: The superficial and initial EK-like structure in the first tooth generation in shark appears similar to the superficial IK in mice.
source: In the shark, the superficial and initial EK-like structure in the first tooth generation appears similar to the superficial IK in mice.
evidence: Comparative inference drawn from expression patterns between shark and mouse.

claim: The mammalian EK is unable to respond to the Fgf signals which it emits as it lacks Fgf receptors.
source: Importantly, the mammalian EK itself is unable to respond to the Fgf signals, which it emits as it lacks Fgf receptors (Kettunen et al., 1998).
evidence: Cited from published studies on mammalian EK properties.

claim: Fgf receptors in mammals are found within adjacent dental epithelial cells and are important for the induction of differential proliferation between the EK and surrounding epithelial tissue.
source: Instead, these receptors are found within adjacent dental epithelial cells, and are important for the induction of differential proliferation between the EK and surrounding epithelial tissue (Kettunen et al., 2000).
evidence: Cited from published studies on Fgf receptor localization and function.

claim: Apoptosis has been implicated as an important developmental process in regulating the silencing of embryonic signalling centres.
source: Apoptosis has been implicated as an important developmental process in regulating the silencing of embryonic signalling centres (Kettunen et al., 2000; Vaahtokari et al., 1996).
evidence: Cited from published studies on apoptosis in developmental signalling.

claim: TUNEL assays have revealed a lack of apoptosis within the inner dental epithelium of reptiles and the catshark.
source: Such assays have so far revealed a lack of apoptosis within the inner dental epithelium of reptiles (Buchtová et al., 2008; Handrigan and Richman, 2010) and the catshark (Debiais-Thibaud et al., 2015)
evidence: Cited from published studies on apoptosis in non-mammalian teeth.

claim: Mice develop cusps following the loss of apoptosis in caspase-3 deficient mice.
source: However, it has also been shown that mice develop cusps following the loss of apoptosis in caspase-3 deficient mice (Matalova et al., 2006).
evidence: Cited from published studies on caspase-3 deficient mice.

claim: Apoptosis is not fundamentally required in the formation of dental cusps.
source: Although morphological defects are identified in non-apoptotic mouse molars (Matalova et al., 2006), these results suggest that apoptosis is not fundamentally required in the formation of dental cusps (Richman and Handrigan, 2011).
evidence: Inference drawn from studies on apoptosis-deficient mice.

claim: bmp4 may play a role in restricting the expression of other signalling molecules to the EK in the shark.
source: bmp4 expression in surrounding tissues suggests that unlike in mammals, where Bmp4 is secondarily upregulated within the EK, bmp4 may play a role in restricting the expression of other signalling molecules to the EK in the shark.
evidence: Inference drawn from bmp4 expression patterns in shark compared to mammals.

claim: shh may be regulating polarised growth of the catshark tooth along the oral/aboral axis, but not the medial/lateral axis along which the cusps form.
source: It is possible that shh is playing a similar role in teeth of sharks; shh may be regulating polarised growth of the tooth along the oral/aboral axis, but not the medial/lateral axis along which the cusps form.
evidence: Speculation based on shh expression patterns and known functions in other developmental contexts.

claim: Chondrichthyan dental morphology is highly variable between species.
source: Chondrichthyan dental morphology is highly variable between species (Corn et al., 2016; Jambura et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from published studies on chondrichthyan tooth diversity.

claim: Variation in chondrichthyan tooth shape is typically observable as a modification of the cusp.
source: Variation in chondrichthyan tooth shape is typically observable as a modification of the cusp.
evidence: General observation from comparative anatomy studies.

claim: Canonical Wnt pathway signalling lies upstream of EK signalling during mammalian molar morphogenesis.
source: Canonical Wnt pathway signalling is known to lie upstream of EK signalling during mammalian molar morphogenesis, with its upregulation and downregulation leading to supernumerary EKs and the formation of blunted cusps, respectively (Järvinen et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2008).
evidence: Cited from published studies on Wnt signalling in mammalian tooth development.

claim: Alterations to the canonical Wnt pathway may underlie the natural diversity of tooth shape found between chondrichthyan species.
source: As a result, we speculate that alterations to the canonical Wnt pathway may also underlie the natural diversity of tooth shape found between chondrichthyan species.
evidence: Speculation based on experimental results showing Wnt effects on tooth shape.

claim: Odontodes (tooth-like structures) are thought to have initially evolved outside of the oral cavity, with teeth arising through co-option of the underlying odontode gene regulatory network.
source: Odontodes (tooth-like structures) are thought to have initially evolved outside of the oral cavity, with teeth arising through co-option of the underlying odontode gene regulatory network (Donoghue and Rücklin, 2016; Fraser et al., 2010; Martin et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from published evolutionary hypotheses on tooth origins.

claim: Dermal denticles and teeth are deeply homologous, sharing a high degree of structural and developmental conservation.
source: Dermal denticles (non-regenerative odontodes present on the skin surface of chondrichthyans) and teeth are deeply homologous, sharing a high degree of structural and developmental conservation (Cooper et al., 2018; Cooper et al., 2017; Martin et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from published studies on dermal denticle and tooth homology.

claim: Identical expression patterns for fgf3, bmp4, and shh are observed within and around the apical tip of developing teeth and dermal denticles in the catshark.
source: We observe identical expression patterns for fgf3, bmp4, and shh, within and around the apical tip of developing teeth (Figure 3; Figure 5) and dermal denticles in the catshark (Cooper et al., 2018; Cooper et al., 2017).
evidence: Comparison of gene expression patterns between teeth and dermal denticles.

claim: The origin of an apical epithelial signalling centre regulating differential epithelial proliferation in epithelial appendages evolved early within the vertebrate lineage and likely predates the evolution of teeth.
source: As a result, we believe it is likely that the origin of an apical epithelial signalling centre regulating differential epithelial proliferation in epithelial appendages evolved early within the vertebrate lineage and likely predates the evolution of teeth.
evidence: Inference drawn from comparative expression patterns across different epithelial appendages.

claim: The authors propose a new term 'apical epithelial knot' (AEK) to reflect the conservation of the signalling unit across disparate developmental structures.
source: Therefore, to account for this regulation of shape among disparate developmental structures, we propose a new term to reflect the conservation of this signalling unit, the 'apical epithelial knot' (AEK).
evidence: Proposal based on comparative analysis of signalling centres across structures.

claim: Mammalian-specific gene expression patterns within the EK are lineage-specific modifications of an ancestral signalling centre (AEK) that likely evolved prior to the appearance of oral teeth.
source: We therefore suggest that mammalian-specific gene expression patterns within the EK are merely lineage-specific modifications of an ancestral signalling centre (AEK) that likely evolved prior to the appearance of oral teeth.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comparative analysis across vertebrate lineages.

claim: There is an overall increase in dental morphological complexity throughout evolution, culminating in mammals which possess multiple regionalised tooth types (heterodonty).
source: It is generally observed that there is an overall increase in dental morphological complexity throughout evolution, culminating in mammals which possess multiple regionalised tooth types (heterodonty) (Jernvall and Thesleff, 2012; Kavanagh et al., 2007; Tucker and Fraser, 2014).
evidence: Cited from published reviews on dental evolution.

claim: A trade-off between tooth morphological complexity and dental regenerative ability is thought to exist within the mammalian lineage.
source: A trade-off between tooth morphological complexity and dental regenerative ability is thought to exist within the mammalian lineage, with precise occlusion favoured at the expense of dental regeneration (Jernvall and Thesleff, 2012).
evidence: Cited from published hypothesis on mammalian dental evolution.

claim: Dental development is tightly regulated via interactions between the oral epithelium and underlying neural-crest derived mesenchyme.
source: Dental development is tightly regulated via interactions between the oral epithelium and underlying neural-crest derived mesenchyme (Zhang et al., 2005).
evidence: Cited from published studies on dental development.

claim: Canonical Wnt, fibroblast growth factor (Fgf), hedgehog (Hh), bone morphogenetic protein (Bmp), and Notch signalling pathways have all been implicated as important regulators of tooth development and morphogenesis.
source: Canonical Wnt, fibroblast growth factor (Fgf), hedgehog (Hh), bone morphogenetic protein (Bmp), and Notch signalling pathways have all been implicated as important regulators of tooth development and morphogenesis (Thesleff and Sharpe, 1997).
evidence: Cited from published reviews on tooth development signalling.

claim: A unifying characteristic for the progression of vertebrate tooth development is the high level of cellular expression of developmental keystone genes.
source: Importantly, a unifying characteristic for the progression of vertebrate tooth development is the high level of cellular expression of developmental keystone genes (Hallikas et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from published studies on gene expression in tooth development.

claim: Morphogenesis of epithelial appendages can be driven via differential proliferation rates.
source: This process can be driven via differential proliferation rates (i.e., teeth Jernvall et al., 1994; Salazar-Ciudad and Jernvall, 2010), cell shape changes (i.e., intestinal crypt Sumigray et al., 2018), or cell migration (i.e., hair Ahtiainen et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from published studies on epithelial morphogenesis mechanisms.

claim: The EK is molecularly identifiable as non-proliferative and expresses Wnt, Bmp, Fgf, and Hh markers in mammals.
source: The EK is molecularly identifiable as non-proliferative and expresses Wnt, Bmp, Fgf, and Hh markers (Jernvall and Thesleff, 2012).
evidence: Cited from published characterization of mammalian EK.

claim: Fgf signalling drives differential proliferation between the EK and rapidly proliferating adjacent dental epithelium, leading to folding of the epithelium at the site of dental cusps and the formation of the final tooth shape in mammals.
source: Fgf signalling drives differential proliferation between the EK and rapidly proliferating adjacent dental epithelium, leading to folding of the epithelium at the site of dental cusps and the formation of the final tooth shape (Jernvall et al., 1998; Jernvall et al., 1994; Salazar-Ciudad and Jernvall, 2010).
evidence: Cited from published studies on Fgf function in mammalian tooth development.

claim: During the final stages of dental morphogenesis, the EK dramatically reduces in size as cells undergo apoptosis in mammals.
source: During the final stages of dental morphogenesis, the EK dramatically reduces in size as cells undergo apoptosis (Jernvall et al., 1998).
evidence: Cited from published studies on mammalian EK fate.

claim: In multi-cuspid teeth, secondary enamel knots (SEK) form at the site of each extra cusp and are thought to be induced by the EK.
source: In multi-cuspid teeth, such as mammalian molars, subsequent signalling centres termed secondary enamel knots (SEK) form at the site of each extra cusp and are thought to be induced by the EK.
evidence: Cited from published studies on secondary enamel knot formation.

claim: Epithelial activation of Wnt/β-catenin signalling results in continuous initiation of new tooth units in mice.
source: For example, epithelial activation of Wnt/β-catenin signalling results in continuous initiation of new tooth units in mice; however, activation of Wnt signalling in the dental mesenchyme has an opposite effect, inhibiting sequential tooth emergence (Järvinen et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from published studies on Wnt signalling in mouse tooth development.

claim: Activation of Wnt signalling in the dental mesenchyme inhibits sequential tooth emergence in mice.
source: For example, epithelial activation of Wnt/β-catenin signalling results in continuous initiation of new tooth units in mice; however, activation of Wnt signalling in the dental mesenchyme has an opposite effect, inhibiting sequential tooth emergence (Järvinen et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from published studies on Wnt signalling in mouse tooth development.

claim: Wnt signalling appears to be a primary upstream regulator of EK patterning in mammals.
source: Whilst over a dozen markers have been described within the mammalian EK, Wnt signalling appears to be a primary upstream regulator of EK patterning (Ahtiainen et al., 2016; Järvinen et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from published studies on Wnt signalling in EK regulation.

claim: Lef1-/- mutants exhibit arrested tooth development during bud stage, with the tooth cap and associated cusps failing to both form and express EK markers, including Fgf4, Shh, and Bmp4.
source: Lef1-/- mutants exhibit arrested tooth development during bud stage, with the tooth cap and associated cusps failing to both form and express EK markers, including Fgf4, Shh, and Bmp4 (Kratochwil et al., 2002).
evidence: Cited from published studies on Lef1 mutant mice.

claim: Fgf4 is capable of rescuing tooth development in Lef1-/- mutants.
source: Fgf4 is capable of rescuing tooth development in Lef1-/- mutants (Kratochwil et al., 2002).
evidence: Cited from published rescue experiments in Lef1 mutant mice.

claim: The inhibition of Wnt signalling during early bud stage via ectopic expression of Dkk1 leads to blunted cusps and a reduction in Bmp4 signalling.
source: Furthermore, the inhibition of Wnt signalling during early bud stage via ectopic expression of the Wnt antagonist Dickkopf-related protein 1 (Dkk1) leads to blunted cusps and a reduction in Bmp4 signalling (Liu et al., 2008).
evidence: Cited from published studies on Dkk1 effects on tooth development.

claim: Mesenchymal-specific knock-down of Bmp4 leads to a reduction in Lef1 expression.
source: However, more complex feedback loops are involved, as mesenchymal-specific knock-down of Bmp4 (Bmp4ncko/ncko) also leads to a reduction in Lef1 expression (Jia et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from published studies on Bmp4 knock-down effects.

claim: In reptiles, there appears to be no clear histologically definable EK.
source: In the subset of reptiles studied to date, there appears to be no clear histologically definable EK (Buchtová et al., 2008; Weeks et al., 2013)
evidence: Cited from published studies on reptile tooth development.

claim: In some reptile species, there is a thickening of the inner dental epithelium which leads to the asymmetric deposition of enamel and the formation of cusps.
source: although in some species there is a thickening of the inner dental epithelium which leads to the asymmetric deposition of enamel and the formation of cusps (Zahradnicek et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from published studies on reptile tooth development.

claim: In reptiles, cells of the inner dental epithelium are non-proliferative, but this region is not as highly restricted to the cusp as in mammalian molars.
source: Furthermore, whilst in reptiles, cells of the inner dental epithelium are non-proliferative, this region is not as highly restricted to the cusp as in mammalian molars (Buchtová et al., 2008; Handrigan and Richman, 2011).
evidence: Cited from published studies on reptile tooth development.

claim: There is conservation of signalling within an EK-like signalling centre in reptiles.
source: However, there is conservation of signalling within an EK-like signalling centre (Richman and Handrigan, 2011).
evidence: Cited from published studies on reptile tooth development.

claim: Similar EK-like signalling centres have been described in teleosts.
source: Similar EK-like signalling centres have been described in teleosts, with chemical perturbation of these signalling pathways resulting in shifts in cusp number (Fraser et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from published studies on teleost tooth development.

claim: In sharks and rays, there is a region of non-proliferative cells within the apical dental epithelium thought to be associated with the primary cusp.
source: In sharks and rays, there is a region of non-proliferative cells within the apical dental epithelium thought to be associated with the primary cusp (i.e., the primary enameloid knot; Rasch et al., 2020; Rasch et al., 2016)
evidence: Cited from published studies on shark and ray tooth development.

claim: The presence of a definitive EK in sharks has not yet reached a consensus.
source: however the presence of a definitive EK has not yet reached a consensus (Debiais-Thibaud et al., 2015)
evidence: Cited from published debate on shark EK presence.

claim: Some have argued that the EK is uniquely a mammalian innovation.
source: and some have even argued that the EK is uniquely a mammalian innovation (Handrigan and Richman, 2011; Handrigan and Richman, 2010; Richman and Handrigan, 2011; Weeks et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from published arguments on EK evolution.

claim: The diversity in tooth shape in the elasmobranchs is vast, ranging from flattened tooth units associated with crushing prey items, to multi-cuspid and serrated tooth units necessary for cutting.
source: The diversity in tooth shape in the elasmobranchs is vast, ranging from flattened tooth units associated with crushing prey items, to multi-cuspid and serrated tooth units necessary for cutting (Jambura et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from published studies on elasmobranch tooth diversity.

claim: There is a significant increase in the variation of dental shapes across the PC1 axis following Wnt downregulation with IWR-1-endo relative to DMSO control teeth.
source: When looking at the variation in tooth shapes between individual teeth (not averaged by sample), we observe a significant increase in the variation of dental shapes across the PC1 axis (38.2% of overall variation) following Wnt downregulation with IWR-1-endo (pairwise F-test: F41,47=0.277, p<0.001) (Figure 6—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of individual tooth shape variation.
